answer.rationale: The strongest causal signal is temporal: write-path p99 began climbing ~90 minutes ago, a release shipped ~120 minutes ago. Rollback addresses a plausible root cause rather than masking symptoms, and it is the only candidate that both restores the prior known-good state and does not endanger in-flight writes. Regional failover is explicitly ruled out: memory_b2 records that it recovered latency fast but opened a 40-minute replication gap with two accounts losing writes, and the carve-out is 'never fail over while writes are hot' — settlement traffic is at daily peak, exactly the prohibited condition, and losing customer writes violates the primary objective. add_capacity (memory_b3) succeeded against a pre-provisioned demand surge, not a post-release latency regression, and provisioning lead time will not help inside this window. route_read_replicas (memory_b5) relieved read pressure on the primary; the degradation here is on the write path, so it is at best partial and may not touch the cause. enable_circuit_breaker (memory_b4) contained an external partner outage by failing fast — here failing fast on settlement writes would shed exactly the customer writes we are told to protect. I want two archived records before committing. memory_b1 is the record my action rests on: I need the original to know whether that rollback was clean under load or during a quiet window, and specifically whether the release carried schema or data migrations, since rolling back a migration while settlement writes are hot is the one way this action could itself destroy writes. memory_b6 is the strongest disconfirmer: if staged gating and canary cohorts reliably surface regressions within an hour, then this release passing to GA is evidence against it being the cause, and I should suspect a load-dependent effect that canary volume would not reproduce — which changes how much I trust the temporal correlation. Note that these memories are consolidated summaries; each records a success under conditions that may not match a settlement-peak write regression, and I am treating the correlation between release and onset as suggestive, not established. I therefore intend a guarded, cohort-limited rollback with explicit write-integrity checks and an abort trigger, rather than a fleet-wide revert: if the archived records show a migration in the release, or show canary coverage that genuinely exercised write load, I will not proceed with rollback and will fall back to routing reads off the primary to buy headroom until the next window.
